utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Popovic is continuing with his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D009-0943.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is number 20 in your binder, Mr. Mladenovic. Yes, that's the document, Mr. Mladenovic. Before we start with a brief analysis of this are report, could you please look at the second page and tell me whether that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is a report about a contact with verifiers of the OSCE Mission. The date is the 2nd of February, 1999. I would like to ask you to focus on the middle of the first page of this report where you say: "In response to my comment that we don't know what this was all about but the citizens often do not know enough and, therefore, due to misinformation or lack of information on the part of citizens, there is a tendency of misinterpreting events" et cetera. Could you please tell us what you meant when you wrote this in that report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that propaganda that was aimed at the citizens incessantly. It caused great fear among the citizens, and it is due to that fear that they moved out of the area. So we made every conceivable effort to alleviate that fear and not to have false stories spread because people kept repeating these stories and that caused even greater fear and horror which led to people moving out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm also going to ask you to look at the last paragraph on page 1 of this statement where it says: "I raise my objection and criticised the behaviour of verifiers who on the 1st of February, 1999, went to the crime scene in the village of Gornje Godance ahead of an on-site investigation team." Could you please give us your brief comment. Did that kind of thing happen often?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the beginning when we had these contacts. Tom Olofsson, I told you, he was the commander of the verifiers in Stimlje, and sometimes citizens would directly report crimes to the verifiers, so they went to the crime scene before we did and therefore disrupted it. I drew their attention here to the fact that no one was allowed to do that. They can receive that information, but it's the police that has to go there to secure the scene and the investigation organs have to go and carry out an on-site investigation, and all of that can be watched from the side, as it were. That was our objection. He accepted that, and in the future, that kind of thing did not happen again. They did not go to the scene ahead of us. The police would secure the scene, and they would monitor, observe what the investigation teams did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00822.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D010-0799.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's 21 in your binder, Mr. Mladenovic. First of all, can you confirm to us that you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a report on sighting of or contact with members of the OSCE Mission. The date is the 9th of March, 1999. Could you please look at number 2, or rather, let us look at the first paragraph. Subject of interest and questions that were put in relation to the security barrier. Could I please have your comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on a contact that was established. I cannot remember who was present. Yes, Olofsson again, Sweden. Masi Mammadov from Azerbaijan, and an interpreter from Urosevac. This is what we suggested yet again. Namely that we noticed that there was some strange behaviour on the part of the OSCE verifiers and the members of the KLA. At the house where they stayed, the house that they rented, during the night they had suspicious individuals coming to see them from the forest so they even asked why we put that barrier there in Racak. I think that's what it was all about. Whether there were any objections, so on and so forth. And now whether we placed that check-point or barrier at Cesta for security reasons, and I said that we had not placed that barrier, it was the KLA that placed that barrier there while they were on that locality. Again my comment in respect of this report is that attacks were incessant from that village against our check-point that protected the remaining part of town from incursions from the forest, terrorist incursions. I think that I gave you an appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00823.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have D009-0910.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 22 in your binder. This is a dispatch dated the 14th of March, 1999. We see down here that it says, Stimlje police station commander, senior warrant officer Branko Mladenovic. That's you, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give us your brief comment with regard to the content of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do with information provided to the duty service at the Urosevac SUP to the effect that a terrorist attack had been launched against a vehicle that was moving along the road that we were securing. The vehicle was hit, and a soldier who was in the vehicle was wounded, and it explains what happened to him. Members of the police holding the position the PPO in Crnoljevo Stimlje responded to the attack. I mean, that security check-point had been attacked too. This was a dispatch that was sent to the Urosevac SUP in accordance with that instruction to report and inform on everything significant that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, please, could you repeat -- first of all, PPO Crnoljevo, what is PPO, what is the task of that PPO in Crnoljevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, that is "privremena policijaska stanica" temporary police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a temporary police squad in Crnoljevo. That is a squad that was established in order to secure the road between Pristina and Prizren going via Stimlje and the Crnoljevo gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00824.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D143, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's 23 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, we'd like the documents to appear on the screens. The date of the document is the 1st of April, 1999. Could we please have a brief comment as to what the purpose of this document was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the MUP staff for APKM from Pristina that was sent to all secretariats. As you can see here, inter alia the secretariat in Urosevac, and the police stations in relation to the new situation caused by NATO bombing that started on the 24th of March, 1999, and in order to provide an effective and timely information, it is necessary that you submit a daily summary of important incidents and events for the period from 0600 hours to 0600 hours on the following day to the staff of the ministry of the Republic of Serbia for the AP KiM and fax it to the MUP staff and then the number of the fax by 7.00 a.m. This summary should include the following: Bombing of the NATO forces, date, time, place. Bombing by NATO forces, date, time, place, type, and manner of bombing from aircraft cluster bombs, cruise missiles, et cetera, results, human casualties and material damage. Number 2, terrorist attacks against MUP and Yugoslav Army personnel and facilities, again, date, time, place, type and manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read everything that the document says. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's signed by General Sreten Lukic. This is a standard dispatch that was sent in relation to our obligation vis-a-vis the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, I would particularly be interested in paragraph 4 of this document, that is to say, persons of Albanian ethnicity who fled from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. First of all, did you keep records of these persons in the period when this dispatch was sent, the 1st of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not keep records because it was impossible to keep records of that kind. It was impossible for a simple reason, because practically everybody was fleeing from the theatre of war. Serbs, Albanians, Roma, Turks, everybody else. Especially women and children. Everyone sought shelter. Some went in the direction of Serbia, others went in the direction of Albania, yet others in the direction of Macedonia. They all went to stay with their relatives or wherever else they could stay. I mean, I sent my own family to Serbia. So that was the situation. In all that panic, it was impossible to keep accurate records of the number of persons who had fled from the area. There were columns moving all time in different directions. If we were to do that at check-points then we would actually be keeping the columns too long. They would be delayed, and the bombing was indiscriminate. A bomb could fall anywhere at any point in time, so that was the reason why that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take this in the right order. First of all, tell me, were you born in the province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have friends among Albanians and other ethnic groups living in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I had many Albanian friends, Sadri Sulja [phoen] was my next door neighbour, and we lived as if we were all one family, one household. I had lots of friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see columns of refugees going through Stimlje or in the territory of the police station of Stimlje, and if so, how big were these columns and which direction were they moving?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw columns of refugees. They were ethnic Serbs and Albanians, and I had occasion to talk to them. Our appeal was for them to stay, however, as I said, I sent my own family away, so it's not that we could insist. Columns were moving in the direction of Albania, Serbia, Macedonia, wherever people thought that they could find shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked to these people, did you ask them what the reasons were, why they were leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the bombing that was the main reason, the danger of bombing. Then there was another very important reason. They didn't want to be caught in cross-fire between members of the police or the army, and the members of the KLA. These were two important reasons. There were other reasons as well. There was the danger of using -- of having depleted uranium bombs used. A lot of people were talking about that. Everybody knew how dangerous uranium was, then also cluster bombs were used. So that would be about it, those would be the reasons involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you have any information percentage-wise as to how many ethnic Serbs left the territory of Stimlje in March, April, and May, 1999, that is to say, before June?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, you mean ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, ethnic Serbs. How many ethnic Serbs left the territory of Stimlje in the period of March, April, and May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what the exact figure was, but I think that practically the entire population left. Only the men stayed behind taking care of their homes. At first, the women and children were there seeking shelter in basements and the like, but ultimately they all left. Just very few people stayed, and everybody left by the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you left Stimlje on the 12th of June, as you said, what happened it to that mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque remained intact. Wherever the police was deployed and where the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just intervene here. I should have done this from yesterday, but it goes on and on. I don't think this is in the 65 ter of the -- that was presented to us. This is what I'm told. I also know that much of evidence led yesterday in respect to what happened at the Stimlje police station on the 15th was not in the 65 ter. I desisted, I did not intervene at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness is speaking about the situation of the territory of the Stimlje police station during the NATO bombing. The question sought to elicit information about the mosque in Stimlje under the jurisdiction of the police station there, and I don't see how this goes beyond what was announced as the contents of this witness's statement. Why should matters relating to the mosque be special as opposed to everything else in the territory of the Stimlje police station in March, April, and May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem arises, Mr. Popovic, because your summary is so short and general. Words like a witness will testify about the situation in Stimlje and the territory of Urosevac, full stop. Now, that gives no indication of the nature of the evidence to be led, the issues to be covered, and that is the sort of thing that you put here as a summary. The problem is a failure to comply reasonably with the requirements of the rule as to notice. Carry on with what you are doing, but if it is the case that the Prosecution is not in a position to deal with all aspects that have been covered in the evidence in chief, inevitably a request by them for an adjournment of their cross-examination will be met, and it may mean the witness will have to stay here until such time as the Prosecution have been able to prepare adequately to deal with the range of matters that are dealt with in the evidence. Now, that position is being taken today in respect of this witness. Can we suggest that you look at the summaries of witnesses to come to see whether they really are giving a reasonable warning of the nature of the evidence and the matters to be dealt with in the evidence. If they are not, the summary should be supplemented to give the Prosecution adequate warning. Carry on for the moment, and you've heard Mr. Stamp and our position about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will certainly act in accordance with your instructions. Should we receive any request from the OTP, we will certainly also give them the information they want. I have no more question about this topic. I will continue in connection with the mosque. If there should be subsequent situations, such situations with witnesses, we will inform the OTP accordingly if the summary should not have been detailed enough. Let us now please look at Exhibit D698.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That is tab 24, Mr. Mladenovic. Mr. Mladenovic, this is a flyer, and here is my question: Did you have an opportunity to see such flyers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see this flyer. It was red with black print on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the only kind of flyer that you were able to see in the territory of KiM during the NATO bombing, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not the only flyer. There were various flyers. Some were dropped from planes, others were glued on houses and lamp posts, et cetera. There were various flyers with different content. All of them were meant to instill fear, all these flyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I believe that the consequence was exactly as intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at D007-122.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 27, sir. Yes, this is the document. Mr. Mladenovic, please take a look at page 6 first, and I would also like for page 6 in the B/C/S version to be displayed. I suppose the page reference is the same for the English language version. Mr. Mladenovic, do take a look at the last paragraph here which starts with "on the 5th of April, 1999." I don't want to read it out to you, so read it to yourself and tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about an incident at the beginning of the bombing when total chaos broke out. There were many broken shop windows and much damage everywhere. There was theft from shops and for abuse of official position, we also arrested some police officers. It says here, On the 5th of April, 1999, and all the way through the paragraph, or rather, in the -- to the beginning of the next page in the original, the names are mentioned here. Can I read out the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Stanojevic; Canovic [phoen], Miomir; Mitrovic, Slavisa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Some names escaped us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then Slavisa Stakic from Stimlje also. All those who had broken the law during the bombing. Although they were police officers at such difficult times in the war when we needed every single police officer we had, we launched a criminal proceedings or misdemeanour proceedings or disciplinary proceedings against them. I know about this case because I gave orders that proceedings be taken against them. They were detained for awhile, I don't know exactly how long, and there were criminal reports filed against them, what they -- Prosecution office in charge, and the -- our superior authority at Urosevac was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00825.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to see a document which is under seal now. I believe that we can see it the same way as we proceeded yesterday. It's D142. I only have two questions about some sentences in that document, and it is important that only we in the courtroom see it and nobody outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document is only to be displayed in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is tab 26, Mr. Mladenovic. It's an Official Note. You can see the date. Please read the last paragraph of this Official Note, and comment it for us, especially the mention of cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an Official Note which was made during the bombing on the 11th of May, 1999. This was standard procedure. The event in question was registered with the Stimlje police station, and it is about an attack carried out by NATO airplanes. They attacked the security check-point of Kostanje in Stimlje, and they dropped cluster bombs. Four persons were seriously wounded and four members of the VJ who after first aid was administered to them were transferred to the Pristina hospital. Only on the following day when we were able to get there in the afternoon, we found another soldier who had been killed. So this document speaks about an event during the NATO bombing, and it is -- it proves that cluster bombs were dropped. Those wounded were wounded very badly by these bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. D146, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 29, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is not under seal, so it can be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, this is an Official Note dated the 27th of May, 1999, and it says that certain persons were brought to the Stimlje police station for an interview. Was that regular procedure, and what happened to those persons after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regular procedure, standard procedure. All units in the area of the Stimlje police station were duty-bound to apprehend every person that threatened them and take them to the Stimlje police station. So this document speaks about the VJ which was in the area, I cannot tell exactly where, yes, Gornje Godance that they found some persons that they thought were suspicious and brought them to Stimlje police station. An Official Note was drafted about that by Dragan Gojkovic who at the time was a police officer at Stimlje police station. One such note with this list was also forwarded to the OKP of the Urosevac SUP. They treated these persons additionally, and if there was no reason to detain them, they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the following page, please. We see that on the 28th of May an interview was conducted with Salih Nuredini, and if you look at the previous page you will see that under 16 his name is mentioned. This is the English version so we see under 16 Salih Nuredini.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you go back one page, or forward. All right. No, this is the first page. In English we need the following page. We need Salih Nuredini's statement. While we are waiting for that, you take a look at the statement, Mr. Mladenovic, and tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see here in the first paragraph it says this statement was taken on the 28th of May, 1999, from Salih Nuredini from the village of Zborce in the Stimlje municipality where he has permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, this document, statement appears not to be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that there is no translation of the statement which is part of the original document. Although this document is already an exhibit, but it was admitted as is, I move that the Defence should make a translation of this statement of Salih Nuredini who was also on the list of the persons apprehended on page 1. Since there is no English translation available, I will now refrain from asking the witness questions about that statement. It was -- he was only meant to be corroborate that this was the same person anyway, and I will contact the translation service and apply for a translation, which we will submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, in 1998 and 1999 did you ever see or hear of the existence of a plan or agreement in the framework of the MUP under which the Albanian population was to be expelled from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I have never heard of it, I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever in 1998 or 1999 see or hear that there was a plan or an agreement in the framework of the MUP to the effect that the ethnic structure of Kosovo should be changed by expelling the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen or heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I conclude with my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, can you tell us, please, what position do you occupy now in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I am chief of the department for foreign nationals suppressing illegal immigrations and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the police administration in Smederevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just please repeat what your job is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am head of the department for foreign nationals for suppressing illegal immigrations and human trafficking at the police administration in Smederevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have a rank in the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, we have ranks in the sense of titles now, so it used to be the rank of major, but now I'm senior chief inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us in your evidence yesterday that there were reserve branch police stations, and you described what these were. And you said they had no base, no physical base, I think you meant. When you referred to these reserve branch stations, did you mean the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that they didn't have a separate office of their own or a facility where they had to come and report, and then leave. That's what I meant. They had weapons they had received as members of the reserve police force and they kept these weapons at home. So members of this reserve police squad were at their homes. We had them in Muzicane and Godance, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Just please try to confine yourself to what I've asked you. So we are talking about the reserve police squads then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve police squads. [B/C/S spoken], that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And you told us that they were organised by reserve police officers, and you also told us that these were villagers who were self-organised. Can you explain what might apparently be a conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to that number of reserve policemen who were engaged in the police station in Stimlje, there were others whose obligation was to be reserve policemen, but they were not engaged in the police station. They had their weapons that they had been issued with, they kept these weapons at home, and they guarded their own homes, their own villages. That's it. That's the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So these were not policemen, these were villagers who had been organised to protect their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said they were armed. Who armed them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As military conscripts, they were armed at the police department or the Ministry of the Interior through the inspector or rather, officer who was in charge of the reserve force. They were all military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So they were armed as far as you know by the relevant officials of the police department of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac for our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of arms or weapons they were issued?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that they just had light infantry weapons, rifles and pistols, that is. Nothing else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the exercise or the discharge of your responsibilities as chief of the police station in Stimlje, did you have to work with any of these squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not chief of the police station, I was commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. As commander of the police station, did you in the -- in your work have to deal with these squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept them under control because we sent police patrols, regular police patrols every day to see them. And their duty was as follows: If they were attacked or in jeopardy, they were supposed to notify us via radio transmitters that they received from the police about such an attack so that we could help them on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the MUP also provide them with these radio station facilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you said you kept them under control, could you explain a little bit more. What was the responsibility of the MUP to keep these reserve police squads under control?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it meant that persons who had weapons should not abuse them in any way, so we monitored that. We were vigilant so that there would be no abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it was the responsibility of the active MUP officers to ensure that these civilians who had received these weapons use them according to the law?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who, if you can recall, was the MUP official in the area of your police station that was responsible for exercising control, or most responsible for exercising control over these RPOs in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Gradimir Zivic, a police officer. I think that was his name. He belonged to the police department of the Urosevac SUP. Not the police station of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Can you spell his name, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Z, with a diacritic, i-v-i-c with a diacritic G-r-a-d-i-m-i-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said that they were composed, that is reserve police squads, of both Serbs and Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said, if I can find where I noted it, that in respect to the Albanians, and I'll quote: "I now cannot remember everybody's names, but I remember the families Qeremi and Olluri, they were all of them practically involved. I didn't have the list nor did I keep a register." Can you tell me or tell the Court approximately many Kosovo Albanians were engaged in these reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I said Karimi, I said Qeremi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My fault, I'm sorry. Qeremi. And Olluri, is that the right pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many Kosovo Albanians, can you recall, approximately were involved in these reserve police squads in 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the exact numbers. For example, from the Olluri family, there was Hysen Olluri with his three brothers, Nazmi, I can't remember the names of the rest of them. I know it was the four of them, four brothers. From the Qeremi family, Bedri was an active policeman, his father, I can't remember his exact name now, and another brother, I think. Fatmir worked at the police station in Lipljan as an active policemen, so it was from these families. I cannot give you the exact numbers just off the cuff because I don't know exactly how many of them there were, but I know that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the villages that you remember in your area that had the bulk of these reserve squads, and pardon my pronunciation, I may get it wrong, you said Muzicane?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muzicane, that's the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Rasince?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasince.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I might get this one right, Gornje Godance, right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Donje Godance.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These were Serbian villages, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were multi-ethnic villages, they were not purely Serb villages. The majority population in these villages was Albanian. There were a few ethnic Serbs in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But it was the ethnic Serbs who were armed; am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the Serbs were armed, but there were also Albanians who were, that is to say that there were Albanians too, but most of the armed persons were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can -- the reserve police squads were created in the middle of 1998; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About the middle, approximately 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember the exact date, and I don't want to engage in guess-work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at P901.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document from General Pavkovic who at the time was the commander of the Pristina Corps, and the time is the 26th of June, 1998. And it is about the arming of these RPOs. Do you recall that the RPOs were armed by both the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just -- I'm not asking about the bona fides of the document right now. You recall that the RPOs were armed by both the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that at all. I really don't know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know that the MUP, I think you said that before, was involved in arming the RPOs. Do you know that the VJ also was involved in arming the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know that what I said a few moments ago, that the police had as its reserve force, it's reservists, and that they armed them. As for what the army did, I really don't know. Maybe they did do this, but I really don't know. I cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, I think, that these reserve police squads were composed of persons who were both military and police conscripts.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I've been misunderstood. Everybody is a military conscript, including us, members of the police. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you said that these persons were reserve police officers or reserve soldiers, and they were armed as all of the members of the reserve forces of either the police or the army. This is at 12463, line 13 to 16 yesterday. You recall, Mr. Mladenovic, that some of the members of these RPOs were military conscripts who had not been mobilised as yet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see what this is all about, I have to explain this. Obviously you don't understand me. All persons who had served their military service after doing that become military conscripts. Part of the military conscripts belong to the reserve police force, whereas the rest are military conscripts and have military duty vis-a-vis the Army of Yugoslavia. The reserve police force was armed by the police whereas this other part, the military conscripts, now, whether the army armed them or not, that, I don't know. And in which way they did that or they were just military conscripts without weapons, just like the reserve force that is unarmed. I really cannot go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's look at this document at paragraph 6. Can you see paragraph 6 there? I'll read it because paragraph 6 on the English copy goes from page 1 to page 2. Do you have paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just move a little bit to the left on the B/C/S copy so we could be able to see the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to see the paragraph numbers in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He says in respect to the distribution of the weapons, and we'll get back to that, "After completing distribution, prepare and organise inhabited places for defence. The military department commanders are responsible for organising this -- move on to page 2 in the English -- for organising this in their zones of responsibility in co-operation with the MUP and local self-government organs. Form units in each village according to the military structure: In squads, platoons, and companies." Now, does this help you, Mr. Mladenovic, that these squads were formed in co-operation with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember at all that there was this kind of thing. I'm telling you that I've never seen this document. I never had an opportunity to meet someone from the army and agree on matters of this nature. At my station, I never received this kind of document, I've never seen any such thing or did I have anything to do with any such thing. The army, that is. They had their own chain of command, their own command, I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You have told us already that you haven't seen the document before. Let me ask you this: In the organisation of the RPOs, as you know them, do you know of any VJ involvement in your area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of that, not in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were some of the members of the RPOs in your area issued with automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, light machine-guns, sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that they received infantry weapons as prescribed. I meant rifles. I don't know exactly which kinds, but there were automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not sure, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many RPOs, reserve police squads, were in the area of the jurisdiction of the Stimlje police in 1999, let me narrow it down a bit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two in Muzicane with Rasince and the village of Godance, Gornje Godance and Donje Godance that is, and Petrovic. That was one police squad. I think it was only those two. I don't think that there were any more in the territory of the police station of Stimlje, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many were in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Urosevac is a big city, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many were within the SUP of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was roughly the information that I had at the police station of Stimlje. It was only for the police station of Stimlje. I don't know about the rest because in the territory of the SUP of Urosevac, there was the police station of Urosevac, OUP Kacanik, and the Strpci police station. These are big areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look a P1055.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we move on to the next document, I simply have to react since when this document was being introduced P901, my learned friend Mr. Stamp said that it had do with arming reserve police squads. I think -- it's not that I think, I'm sure, there is no mention whatsoever of such squads in this document anywhere. I simply think that this is an unfair line of questioning. I think the answer doesn't matter any more whether it works in favour of the Defence or the Prosecution. I simply think that dealing with matters in this way is not in the interest of these proceedings not going into the witness's answers at all. There is no mention whatsoever of reserve police squads in this document, not in a single place, and I think that that is so unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution's case is based on this document and many others is that this document refers to the formation of the reserve police squads and that can be substantiated by a lot of evidence from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does the document suggest that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document itself does not say reserve police squads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. It was put to the witness without any qualification, Mr. Stamp. You didn't get him to comment on whether it was a document referring to reserve police squads, and the questions you put about it suggested that it was. Now, you can see the basis for the objection of unfairness in that, so would you please bear that in mind in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will just, without making much of it, I think my question and the introduction is at page 21 of the record. If we could look at P1055.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 16th of February, 1999 to the Chief of Staff, to the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. Do you recall in mid-February there was -- there were visits from members of the MUP staff in order to audit the work of the RPOs in the various secretariats?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any audits by the staff in my police station. I had no opportunity to see this document, this is some sort of dispatch, but it has to do with Pristina. The Pristina secretariat is sending a dispatch to the staff in Pristina as far as I can see here. I really know nothing about this. At Stimlje police station there was no meeting involving both the staff and the reserve police squads. That is what I can tell you for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 in B/C/S, page 2 in English. I'm sorry, it is page 1 in B/C/S and the page in English is correct, page 2. It would seem to be the middle of page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to see if you remember, it indicated the purpose of the meetings or the purpose of the visits was to hold meetings with the commanders of the reserve police squads, I think this should be, that were also attended by the chiefs of the secretariats of the interior, police department chiefs, police department officers, and police department's deputy commanders in charge of organisations and functioning of the reserve police squads in their respective areas as well as VJ army officers in charge of defence of towns and villages with the Serbian and Montenegrin population. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the paragraph, but I don't know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm about to ask it. Well, firstly, does this remind you that these reserve police squads were monitored and armed by the VJ as well as the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say based on what I see here in this document, this says that such a meeting was held at the Urosevac MUP and that the chiefs of the departments of police were present and other people, but no commander of any police station. I'm not familiar with this. I don't know these details so I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It also indicates that the meetings were in respect to RPOs that were responsible for the defence of towns and villages with Serbian and Montenegrin population. Do you recall that that was the purpose of [indiscernible] of the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I know that the main reason why they were armed was to enable them to protect their families, no more than that. I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 7, I think, in the English and 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see a chart here with a breakdown of weapons that had been issued in the various municipalities to these RPO members. In item 6 for your secretariat Urosevac, there were 1.928 weapons issued by the MUP and 3.023 weapons issued by the VJ. Are you aware that this -- that this number of weapons had been issued to these persons within the Urosevac secretariat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that any number approximating to this, any number of weapons approximating to this had been issued to these civilians in the Urosevac area, at the SUP Urosevac area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I don't know how many weapons were distributed in the territory of the Urosevac SUP. I never had the opportunity to see anything relating to it, nor did I hear anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we look at the bottom of your page and go to the next page in B/C/S. Sorry, the bottom in B/C/S, the bottom of that page in B/C/S and the next page in English, the first bullet point, about the conclusions reached at the meetings, that they were to urgently hold meetings in all RPOs with the presence of representatives of the MUP, VJ, and municipal staffs. You have told us, Mr. Mladenovic, that your SUP chief would communicate many orders and decisions to you. Did he communicate this conclusion or decision to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never communicated this order to me or a report like this, so I cannot really comment this document. This concerns the Urosevac SUP. I never had the chance to see it or know anything about this. This document was never forwarded to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just trying to use it to see if I can jog your memory, because you are saying that you had SUPs within -- sorry, you had RPOs within your jurisdiction, and many times you received decisions in respect to the areas within your competence from your SUP chief. I am just asking you if in respect to the second bullet point, "to urgently activate regular services in exclusively Serbian communities, as well as reconnaissance, monitoring, and ambush setting services in ethnically mixed communities," if that decision was communicated to you by your SUP chief?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such decision. I was never informed of this, and I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally who was your immediate superior in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the department of the police Radomir Mitic. And the chief of the SUP was Bogoljub Janicijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could both of them be described as your immediate superiors, or is there one that you were directly answerable to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the chief of the SUP was chief for the entire secretariat, and the chief of the department of the police was in charge of police squads and police stations. All orders went through the chief of the department of the police. If I were to receive an order, it would have gone through the chief of the department of the police. That was the chain of command, and I reported to the chief of the department of police, and he would inform the chief of the SUP. Sometimes I would get information directly at meetings that I attended, or sometimes the chief would forward some information about some tasks, but not what we are talking about now. And with regard to this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We know you haven't seen it before, I'm just trying to see if you can remember what happened on the basis of this. During the war, the NATO intervention in 1999, the RPOs were sometimes were used to guard important routes or facilities, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve police squads never secured any facilities. They only guarded their own homes and themselves, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When there were joint operations -- or before I get to that, you know that during the war there were many times joint operations with the VJ and the MUP acting in co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the MUP and the VJ acted in co-ordination. I know that the MUP had its own command through the MUP staff for the AP KiM in Pristina, and there was a chain of command that went down, but I know nothing about a joint command. I never saw a document about it, nor do I know anything about such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about a joint command, Mr. Mladenovic. Are you saying, though, that during the course of the war, there were no anti-terrorist operations where MUP forces acted in co-ordination with the VJ that you know of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that PJPs carried out operations under the command of the staff in Pristina, nothing else. I'm not aware of any joint operations. My police station never carried out such assignments. I believe that this question should be asked to somebody else. My police station only went about its regular jobs and tasks, and I mentioned them, the protection of the lives and the personal security --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P767 very quickly. Or maybe we could take the break and do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, we'll have the first break now and resume at 20 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Last time you were here -- thank you, Your Honours. Last time you were here, Witness, you said that the reserve police squads never guarded any facilities, they only secured their own homes and their own lives, and that was all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at D824.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown this also earlier today.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you just agreed with me that the reserve police squads, your evidence is that the reserve police squads never guarded any facilities, only their own homes and their own lives; does that remain your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at this document, especially the last sentence, is it referring to the reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document refers to temporary police squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the distinction between these temporary police squads and these reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A temporary police squad is established based on the minister's order. At that time it was in line with the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement for the purpose of controlling the road from Stimlje, or rather, from Pristina through Stimlje and Suva Reka to Prizren and all the way to the Crnoljevska gorge. So a temporary police squad is established pursuant to the minister's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are composed of active duty policemen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both active duty and reserve policemen, as in all police stations and squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They didn't have civilians in their ranks as the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any armed civilians. They were all uniformed police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at P767.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This one is, on the face of a document is an order of a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Earlier without any prompting from me, you volunteered to us that you didn't know anything about any Joint Command. Nonetheless, I'd like you to have a quick look at this document. Have you ever seen orders in this format before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. This is a military document of sorts. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at -- well, let's look at the date first. This is in respect to the 15th of April, 1999, and if we could look at page 4 of the English, and I think that's just about page 2 in the B/C/S. In any case, we want to see item 5 and the sentence -- the two bullet points before item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the bullet point before item 5 it's for routing their terrorist forces in the area of Jezerce on the 23rd of April, 1999. If look at item 5 you can see that the task of the units of the Pristina Corps is to support MUP forces in routing and destroying the STS along the axis of Dulje, and you can read on to see the other villages. Were these areas, Dulje in particular, within or close to the area of your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Dulje belongs to the Suva Reka municipality. The village of Petrovo is part of the Stimlje municipality. Budakovo belongs to Nerodimlje. Jezerce, Budakovo, Plesina, they all belong to Urosevac. Nerodimlje, Budakovo, Jezerce, Plesina, all these villages are in the municipality of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, so the axis would have included areas in Urosevac as well as an area in the Stimlje police area of responsibility. Now, do you recall this joint military police operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any joint military police operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war, were there any anti-terrorist operations at all that came to your notice? I mean, within your evidence, Mr. Mladenovic you told us a lot about what your SUP chief told you, what your staff told you, what your department head told you. Did it come to your notice at any time during the war that there were anti-terrorist operations within Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and it was not in my sphere of interest because I was busy doing other work at the Stimlje police station. I didn't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Stimlje police station have an obligation to provide members of the PJP for joint -- well, not necessarily joint, but for anti-terrorist operations conducted by the 124th PJP Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat that the PJP unit, the company at Urosevac carried out its tasks and reported to its command. I as commander of the police station had no communication with the PJP, so I don't know what they did or what kind of work they did in the field. My police station had 11 police officers who were also members of the PJP unit of the Urosevac SUP. I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But when you had to deploy them to be engaged with the Urosevac brigade, that's the 124th Brigade, didn't you know what your 11 men were going to be up to? You didn't know what tasks they were going to perform?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I never knew what they were doing. I only had to provide logistical support, that is inform the persons in question, make sure that they come and place them at the disposal of the unit to which they belong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at item 2 of this document, it is page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First paragraph, the task of the VJ, the Pristina Corps with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar population of Kosovo and Metohija, support the MUP forces in routing and destroying the STS in the area of responsibility. Were you not aware, Mr. Mladenovic, that the VJ, the MUP, and civilians described as armed non-Siptars were engaged in operations within the zone of your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reports or information about that. There were military units in the territory of the municipality of Stimlje, but they had their own command, and they answered to their own command. They had no points in common with us, our police station. We had nothing in common. They did their work, we did our work. I really don't know who was within their composition. We didn't even see each other, as a matter of fact. We knew where everyone was, but they knew that the police station was carrying out its own work, so we did not interfere in each other's work, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not talking about interference. There is a war going on, you are chief of the police station for the municipality -- sorry, commander of the police station for the municipality, and we have here what on the face of it seems to be a major operation along a major axis that cuts into your municipality in Petrovo. Yes, I was right, Petrovo. And you are saying you just did not know at all that this operation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Petrovo is in a forested area to the south-west of Stimlje. It is certainly not on the road where the police was, or did police patrols during the war go to the village of Petrovo Selo, they could not. That part was under the control of the terrorists for awhile and then other units, so we did not go into that forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but remember I'm not asking you if your police or the police that you were commanding directly, were participating in it. I'm just asking you if you as commander even knew about it, and you are saying you never even knew about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn to your police station. There were inspectors of police that sometimes were engaged at your police station. One was Jasovic. Can you tell us his full name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at the Stimlje police station there was no crime police department. Dragan Jasovic is an employee of the crime police department in Urosevac, not in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But did he go down to Stimlje sometimes to conduct investigation and work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was there another one by the name of Sparavalo from Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he also would attend at Stimlje to conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Momcilo Sparavalo, that was his name, was also an employee of the crime police department. They conducted all crime police work in the territory of the police station of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, do you recall that during your testimony when you were being asked questions by counsel for the Defence, you referred to quite a few statements that had been taken by either one or both of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I remember quite a few things that had happened. I cannot remember individually all the persons there, but every person that was brought into custody to the police station on any grounds and that had anything to do with crime, well, an Official Note would be compiled, and it would be recorded in the daily log-book at the duty service station, and the person would be handed over to the OKP inspectors. That was standard procedure that was in force during the bombing and before the bombing throughout my work as commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever in your work as commander of the police station hear of allegations that Jasovic was involved in torturing prisoners, persons who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any allegations --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any allegations that he had been involved in applying electricity to persons who were in the custody of the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In particular, do you -- have you ever heard of any allegation that both Jasovic and Sparavalo beat and tortured including the application of electricity to Kosovo Albanian civilians, suspects on a regular basis? You never heard any allegations like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any such allegations. They had their own superior and their office at the Urosevac SUP, so these persons that we handed over to them they took them over and they conducted interviews at the building of the secretariat in Urosevac, in their offices. They were there under their own superiors, not the police station. I've never heard of all these things that you are talking about, nor did any such thing ever happen at the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there at some point before the NATO intervention a police officer, also a lawyer, who was employed within the Urosevac police SUP by the name of Hebib Koka, K-o-k-a?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally know Hebib Koka. You are referring to Hebib Koka who was an employee of the OUP of Kacanik. As far as I know he was not a police chief, he was an inspector, he was a colleague, he belonged to the OUP of Kacanik. So from Stimlje, that's about 100 kilometres away. Well, perhaps it's not 100, it's about 70, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At some point this police officer worked in Urosevac with Mr. Jasovic and Mr. Sparavalo. Do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they never worked together in the same office, as far as I know. Hebib Koka worked at the OUP Kacanik, and Jasovic and Sparavalo worked at the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know or have you ever heard of any allegations from your former colleague Mr. Koka about the brutality that had been inflicted on the Kosovo Albanians civilians by Mr. Jasovic and Mr. Sparavalo in the course of their work for the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I knew Hebib Koka personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear of that from him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you become aware that he had said or made those allegations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the OSCE, did they ask the questions about allegations of police torturing Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all the things that we discussed with the verifiers. However, everything that we discussed with them is contained in the reports that I submitted. If it is in the report, then that is the case, but I cannot remember right now. As for each and every one of the contacts I had with the verifiers, I compiled a report, so there is a record of what we had discussed. So if there were such questions, that has to be in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that it is possible but you don't remember; is that what you are saying? It is possible that the OSCE representatives raised the issue of beatings and torture of Kosovo Albanians with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that they raised such questions, but I don't remember, and I don't remember any specific case. There has to be a report about such contacts between myself and them and then that would have to be written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could probably look briefly at P1029. It's an OSCE document. The Blue Book. Page 17 in English, which is page 19 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Last sentence: "The KLA commander reported that villagers trying to get to Stimlje or Urosevac are regularly arrested and tortured with electricity in an attempt to get information about the KLA from them." Can you recall the KVM monitors raising these matters with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that that was the case, but right now I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And since we are on this page, you note that in the second sentence it refers to the presence of VJ tanks and artillery close to KLA positions. Were there VJ tanks and artillery, and I'm now directing you to Racak, close to KLA positions in Racak on the 13th of January, which is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see from this document, there is no reference to Racak or to a place where there are tanks. It only says in the area of Stimlje, it said that the tanks and the artillery are within 200 metres of KLA positions. I really don't see where these tanks were, and I don't know what particular place this is referring to. Stimlje is big, 22.000 inhabitants, and then these villages that I mentioned. I cannot really say. And also when --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the document doesn't refer to Racak, but since we were on this page because I'm going to get to that later, and we are going to get to this page, can you recall VJ tanks being in the vicinity of Racak in the days leading up to the operation that began on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that in accordance with the agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke, the road between Stimlje, Crnoljevo, Dulje, that according to that agreement, the army had some authority over that road. They were located in two places. I don't know how to explain this to you now. It's a forest on the right-hand side. Quite opposite in relation to Racak. And they were also in Dulje. Their task was just like of the temporary police squad, to protect the road. That's in accordance with the agreement. And these are small military units at that. I don't even know who they belonged to. So they had their own work there, and that is probably it. And I'm not aware of the tanks and the rest that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How far were these units from Racak on or about the 13th, 12th of January?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how far away as the crow flies, but I could show this to you on a map if you have a map. If you have a map of the area of Stimlje, I can show it to you, but I really wouldn't know what the exact distance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you estimate it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly 5 or 6 kilometres further from Racak, but then there's this hill in front of Racak, so Racak is in a valley and then the hill after that, and the army was here on the other side, on the side opposite in relation to that. And in a forest, in a pine wood at that. And Dulje was in the direction of Suva Reka 20 or 30 kilometres away, so behind the second hill, they were along the road on the other side from Stimlje all the way to Dulje via Petrastica and Zborce. That was where their zone was, so it really had nothing do with our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, 5 to 6 kilometres from Racak you said, approximately. And the second unit at Dulje in the direction of Suva Reka was 20 to 30 kilometres away from Racak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, that's what I can say, but I'm telling you, I'm not sure, I don't have a map in front of me, and I never measured the actual distance. The verifiers knew about that. They perhaps know better what the exact distance was. That was always there from the signing of the agreement until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to the treatment of the civilians. And before we do that, can you just clear up one thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown this document by the attorney for the Defence, and you are explaining that it referred to Kosovo Albanian who you had relayed this story of his treatment by the KLA to the KVM monitors. If you -- you are familiar with this document, I think you wrote it. I just noticed, if you look -- if we look in the middle of the first paragraph, which is about 11 lines up in the English, I see that you refer to this person as a victimised citizen of Albanian nationality. A few lines down, you refer to Siptar terrorists. Two further lines down, you refer to Siptar terrorists. And two lines down in the English copy when you are talking about loyal citizens of the Republic of Serbia, you refer to them as members of the Albanian ethnic community. I just wanted to ask if there's a reason for this distinction between the expression Siptar and the members of the Albanian community? Are you referring to the same ethnicity there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see what this is, in Albanian one says "shqiptar," that is Siptar as translated, Albanian, it's all one in the same thing. So the Albanians themselves say I'm a Siptar. He says "une jam shqiptar." The only difference is in expressing oneself. I'm using both terms because I speak both languages. Sometimes I say Siptar, sometimes I say Albanian. So the translation can be I'm an Albanian, but in Albanian you don't use that actual word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So if we turn to the next page, we see the same theme, like five lines down in the English you refer to Siptar terrorists, in the middle of the page discussing terrorist activities you refer to Siptar terrorists, but then near the end about 10 or 11 lines up in the English, you refer to the citizen of Albanian nationality. That's the one that the police had speaking to the KVM monitors. Your explanation is that you were basically using the two expressions interchangeably, that is the expressions Albanian and Siptar.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, when the Albanians speak themselves, that's what they say. They cannot say it that way. They say Siptar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that the Albanian word is "Siptar" but you wrote a report in Serbian, and I just asked you, you use it interchangeably in this report without any special meaning attached to the word "Siptar"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant one in the same thing here. We in Kosovo who speak both languages often mix expressions from both languages. Many words that we use in Kosovo are not used in Serbia. I can give you some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, but I've heard your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at D140.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is another report you wrote and you use the same interesting language. This was where you were reporting that the KVM observers were indicating that a situation in the area of Stimlje municipality had turned from calm to tense. You recall that was evidence of the person you spoke about spoke about yesterday -- question withdrawn. I will get to that when we are in private session. Let us get to the language here. You see in the first paragraph here, line 11, you use an interesting expression, "armed attacks by Siptar terrorists targeting their fellow Albanians." In that phrase, you are again using the two expressions interchangeably, meaning the same thing.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may not have noticed, but I often use the original abbreviation that they themselves used, the Serbs use, UCK, rather than KLA. I know what it stands for in Albanian, it means translated, Kosovo Liberation Army. It's along the same lines as what I've been explaining for the term Siptar. I've always used the term that was adequate in the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
