utterances.text: Okay. While we are on this document, could I just, Your Honour, go into private session to I may just mention one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the Albanians left because of bombing being caught in a potential cross-fire between the security forces and the KLA, and you mentioned also the use of depleted uranium in the bombing. Can you -- before I ask that question, did you discuss the issue of depleted uranium before you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, discuss with who? With who could I have discussed that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion in relation to your testimony particularly in relation to depleted uranium before you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Depleted uranium, I had an exam at the civil protection faculty. There was a subject of nuclear biologic chemical defence, so I'm informed about depleted uranium. There was absolutely no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... about whether you discussed it in relation to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if there are any strikes using depleted uranium in Stimlje area that came to your attention in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether such weapons were used, but the propaganda, when I spoke about it yesterday, I meant that the propaganda was such that bombs containing depleted uranium would be dropped, and that after that, 4.000 years the area would be uninhabitable. That was propaganda, and of course the intention was to get the population leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My mistake, I thought that perhaps you were saying that there were depleted uranium strikes in Stimlje. When you met these columns of Kosovo Albanians --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one of us saw that, so we don't know whether there were bombs containing depleted uranium and the rest. That was part of the propaganda. And I said that in the area of Drenica there was a radio station which from 3.00 p.m. to 5.00 p.m. I believe daily broadcast propaganda in Albanian. Probably it was an illegal radio station. That's what I spoke about. And there were also flyers that were being scattered to that effect. So this was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are going a little bit beyond. I'm trying to move quickly as well. You said that when you spoke to these Kosovo Albanians who were leaving in the columns during the war, they mentioned the bombing possible cross-fire, and depleted uranium. Did any of them, even one of them, mention that they were afraid of Yugoslav security forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know something, they never contacted me to say that they were afraid of our forces. But they were saying to the Serbs that they were afraid of NATO's bombs and the Albanians. Those were the Serbs that were saying that. And the Albanians were saying that they were afraid of the Serbs. But everybody was equally afraid, Serbs and the Albanians alike. And they all were leaving the area. Even my family and the neighbourhood in Urosevac where we lived also had -- left for fear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, if you confine yourself to answering my questions, we'd spend a much shorter time here. You said that Albanians were saying that they were afraid of the Serbs? Is that what you said? Serb -- well, that is what the record says you said. Did they say that they were afraid of Serbs in general or the armed Serbs and the Serb security forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood me again. It's because of the question you put to me. I wanted to explain that no Albanian ever said to me that they were afraid of Serbs, but rather that they were afraid of the Albanians who were standing up against the Serbs. And they were also afraid of the bombs that were being dropped from planes. That was's what they were saying to us -- to me. And I also -- and I believe that they spoke -- what they were saying to the Albanians was that they were afraid of the Serbs, but I can only assume what they were saying to the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You believe that they were telling their fellow Albanians that they were afraid of the Serbs. How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why, what caused you to conclude that they would be telling their fellow Albanians that they were afraid of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in these reports the verifiers related such information. We got different information from the verifiers. I believe that they were being lied to, that they heard statements such as the Serbs terrorising people rather than the Albanian terrorists terrorising.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Is it not possible, Mr. Mladenovic, that they would be telling this to the verifiers and to their fellow Albanians, but not to you because you were a member of the Serbian security forces, and they were afraid of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that at the police station they -- we also had Albanians who reported that they were -- had been mistreated. I mentioned Ibish Qari, and there were other instances of abductions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't you agree with me that it is possible that the reason why they would be saying to their fellow Albanians and to the KVM monitors that they were afraid of the Serbs but they would not say to you is because you were a police officer and they were afraid of the police; isn't that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disapprove of this question of yours, and I cannot answer it. I said that this was by assumption. You are now putting this question back to me as my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at the flyer again. D6 -- Your Honours, I think I'm reminded that we were supposed to take the break early? Oh, I'm sorry, we haven't reached that point yet. D698, I think. Yes, it is D698.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I want you to understand, Mr. Mladenovic, that I don't for a moment accept that this was a document issued by Mr. Rugova, but it states particularly in the last paragraph or the last two sentences that: "The forces of the KLA are unable to offer resistance to the Serb forces and to defend the Albanian people, and we invite all Albanians threatened by the attack of Serb occupation forces temporarily to evacuate in the direction of Macedonia and Albania." And it is your evidence that this document caused a lot of fear. Wasn't that fear, fear of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when we were discussing one of the reasons that in those days propaganda was widespread, and this flyer is evidence of such propaganda that was disseminated among the civilian population, that they would be caught in cross-fire, and that the KLA was unable to protect them, and that they should evacuate toward Macedonia or around Albania, but the Albanians also went in the direction of Bujanovac and Presevo. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please, I'm going to stop you there. The flyer says the KLA is unable to offer resistance. And they invite people threatened by the attack of the Serb occupational forces to temporarily evacuate, and you said that this flyer, the purpose of this was to instill fear. Wasn't this fear of the Serb security forces? Isn't that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about the propaganda as it was at the time, and this flyer was disseminated in yards and everywhere as propaganda, and I said that I knew this -- I knew this flyer and that it caused a fear and panic in the civilian population. And the consequence of that was not only that the Albanians were leaving, but also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But my question to you on the basis of this flyer is that the flyer, if it caused fear in the Albanian population, it would be because the Albanian population was afraid of the Serb security forces, because that is what the flyer referred to as a threat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this propaganda caused the fear and not what this flyer says. It wasn't just this. There was also the KLA radio that disseminated propaganda, there were planes dropping flyers where the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, no, let's move on to talk about K-86.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think we should do that in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am afraid we need to return to private session. I don't think Mr. Stamp has finished with questions in private session, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you be very long in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hope not, but I think I will be 15, 20 minutes in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't understand you to be saying that Mr. Sainovic did not call the police station that morning, so let me ask you now, do you know about that? Do you know about whether or not Mr. Sainovic called, or are you not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is what I can say. I don't know nor did I ever hear that Mr. Sainovic called up the police station at Stimlje. Nobody ever told me so. That's what I said. I was not going into the issue whether or not he could have called or not. I only said that Sainovic never called up the police station, at least I as commander was never informed of that. If I wasn't there on the 20th, it was either the deputy commander who could have informed me because he was there, he was responsible for the station, and there were two assistants. Nobody ever told me that Mr. Sainovic had called. They only informed me on the 20th that General Djordjevic was present on the 18th. And that's all I know. Whether or not Mr. Sainovic called that morning or whether he called anybody else, that's not a piece of information I ever had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I am finished, but there is some dissent on the Prosecution side as to whether I'm finished. And therefore, I wonder if we could take it now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn overnight again. Mr. Stamp may have more questions for you, Mr. Popovic will, I anticipate. So we must ask you to return again tomorrow. A Court Officer will assist you overnight. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
